summary: Lunar Navigator is an interactive tool that helps explore whether the Sun and Earth are visible from different locations near the Moon's south pole. It uses NASA's LOLA elevation data and JPL SPICE data to study the lunar surface and calculate how the surrounding terrain affects visibility. Users can enter a location and date and time to see if mountains, crater rims or other terrain block the view of the Sun or Earth. The goal is to help people better understand the Moon's surface and support future lunar exploration and site planning.
details: About Lunar Navigator Lunar Navigator is an interactive web application designed to explore whether the Sun and Earth are visible from different locations near the Moon's south pole. It helps users understand how the Moon's surface, including mountains, slopes and crater rims, can block the view of these celestial objects. The application uses NASA's LOLA elevation data and JPL SPICE data to study the lunar terrain and calculate the positions of the Sun and Earth. Users can select a lunar location and a UTC date and time. The application then analyzes the surrounding terrain and shows whether the Sun or Earth is fully visible, partially visible or blocked by the surface. The main benefit of Lunar Navigator is that it makes complex lunar terrain and visibility information easier to explore and understand. This could support early research into possible lunar exploration areas, especially near the south pole, where sunlight and visibility are important factors. The project was developed using Python, Streamlit, Plotly and scientific libraries for working with geographic data and calculations. It uses NASA's LOLA elevation data and JPL SPICE kernels for scientific information. The application is hosted online through Streamlit Community Cloud, allowing people to use it through a web browser. What makes Lunar Navigator creative is the way it combines real lunar elevation data, space science and mathematical calculations in one interactive tool. Instead of simply displaying a map of the Moon, it studies how the actual terrain affects the visibility of the Sun and Earth from a selected location. During development, we considered scientific accuracy, the quality and limits of the available elevation data, the reliability of calculations, ease of use and performance. We also considered situations where the available terrain data might not be enough to give a reliable result. Our goal is to make lunar terrain analysis more accessible and help people better understand some of the challenges involved in exploring the Moon's south pole.
